items.title: An expert-level generalist AI for abdominal CT diagnosis.
items.body: Artificial intelligence (AI) in radiology aspires to deliver expert-level diagnosis across diverse clinical tasks, yet existing supervised strategies remain limited in scope. We developed RADAR, a generalist vision-language model trained on more than 400,000 contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography (CT) examinations and 15 million anatomy-wise image-text pairs, learning directly from clinical reports without manual annotation. Throughout internal and external evaluations across multiple centers and varied clinical scenarios, RADAR achieved high diagnostic performance and robust generalization for 18 anatomical structures and 146 imaging findings. In a reader study, RADAR assistance increased the diagnostic sensitivity of 26 radiologists by ~10%. RADAR offers a scalable, versatile, and interpretable solution for abdominal CT, demonstrating that generalist AI can match human experts in general and complicated radiology tasks.
items.why: This Science paper reports RADAR, a generalist vision-language model trained on more than 400,000 contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography (CT) exams and 15 million anatomy-wise image-text pairs without manual annotation, which achieved high diagnostic performance across 18 anatomical structures and 146 findings in multicenter internal and external evaluations, and increased the diagnostic sensitivity of 26 radiologists by about 10% in a reader study. This is a substantial, well-validated advance in generalist radiology AI with a real clinician-comparison reader study, making it one of the strongest clinical AI results of the week even though it sits outside reproductive medicine.
items.plain: Researchers trained an AI system on over 400,000 abdominal CT scans and their written reports, without needing humans to manually label each finding, and tested it across multiple hospitals for 18 body structures and 146 possible findings. When 26 radiologists used the AI's suggestions, they correctly caught about 10% more true problems than without it, which is a strong, well-tested result for AI helping doctors read scans.

items.title: Real-world use and evaluation of a generative AI chatbot for Parkinson's disease information: a prospective observational study.
items.body: BACKGROUND: Patient-facing medical AI chatbots are entering clinical use faster than evidence can characterise their real-world safety. We evaluated one deployed system and introduce CARE-LLM, a proposed framework for conversation-level post-market surveillance. METHODS: We conducted a prospective, observational, conversation-level evaluation of jAImes, a retrieval-augmented AI information system for Parkinson's disease deployed publicly in Germany, across its first 129 days of operation (Nov 11, 2025-Mar 20, 2026), analysing all 2035 conversations (6146 messages). CARE-LLM (Conversation-level AI Real-world Evaluation) combines automated triage of every conversation, structured expert review of flagged cases, sampling-based sensitivity validation against the adequate class, and a failure-class feedback loop. FINDINGS: AI-assisted triage classified 1803/2035 conversations (88·6%) as good, 224/2035 (11·0%) as partially adequate, and 8/2035 (0·4%) as inadequate. Expert review of 45 flagged conversations confirmed five critical events. Independent re-review of 100 randomly sampled 'good'-rated conversations identified four (4/100, 4%; 95% CI 1·6-9·8) with clinically critical errors missed by the triage-a conditional false-negative rate within the 'good' stratum, not an overall critical-event rate. Confirmed critical events-five flagged, four sampled-spanned three failure classes (knowledge boundary, robustness, and escalation failures) and included an inappropriate memantine recommendation in Parkinson's disease dementia and explicit suicidal ideation that did not trigger the intended emergency response. INTERPRETATION: Tightly scoped, retrieval-augmented, patient-facing AI achieved favourable automated triage classifications while still harbouring clinically critical failures invisible to automated quality metrics alone; detecting them required conversation-level evaluation with clinical expert adjudication. FUNDING: Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft, Interdisciplinary Center for Clinical Research Würzburg, and German Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF); technical development of jAImes was commissioned and financed by Parkinson Stiftung Deutschland.

items.plain: Researchers studied a real chatbot that answers questions about Parkinson's disease, looking at over 2000 real conversations with actual users over about four months. Even though the automatic quality check rated most conversations as good, a closer human review found that some conversations, including ones initially rated as fine, contained dangerous mistakes, like missing a person's suicidal thoughts or suggesting an inappropriate medication, showing that current automatic safety checks alone are not enough.

items.title: The Virtual Biotech: A multi-agent AI framework for therapeutic discovery and development.
items.body: Drug development requires evidence integration across biological scales and modalities, but relevant tools are fragmented. We introduce the Virtual Biotech, an organization of artificial intelligence (AI) agents modeled on a drug-development company, with agentic divisions spanning target discovery, safety assessment, modality selection, and clinical development. We demonstrate its utility at three drug-development decision points. First, over 37,000 agents annotated outcomes from 55,984 trials and found that drugs targeting cell-type-specific genes were 48% more likely to reach market with 32% fewer adverse events. Second, it integrated multimodal evidence to propose a therapeutic strategy in lung cancer. Third, it analyzed a terminated ulcerative colitis trial and inferred potential mechanisms of failure. These results demonstrate that human-guided multi-agent systems can conduct transparent, multiscale analyses to inform therapeutic-development decisions.
items.why: This Science paper introduces the Virtual Biotech, a multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) system in which over 37,000 agents modeled on drug-development roles annotated outcomes from 55,984 trials, finding that drugs targeting cell-type-specific genes were 48% more likely to reach market with 32% fewer adverse events, and it further demonstrated utility in proposing a lung cancer therapeutic strategy and diagnosing a failed ulcerative colitis trial. The scale and transparency of this multi-agent reasoning approach is a notable methodological first for drug development, though the trial-outcome associations are retrospective and correlational rather than prospectively validated.
items.plain: Researchers built a large team of AI programs that each play the role of a different part of a drug company, and used tens of thousands of them to review outcomes from nearly 56,000 past clinical trials. They found that drugs aimed at genes specific to certain cell types succeeded more often and caused fewer side effects, and the same AI team could also suggest a cancer treatment strategy and figure out why a past trial failed, though these findings come from looking backward at existing data rather than testing anything in advance.

glossary.definition: A setup where many AI programs, each handling a different task, work together like departments in an organization.
Unwanted or harmful effects experienced by patients during a medical treatment or trial.
A study design that looks back at existing past data rather than collecting new data as events happen.

items.title: Rapid patient-specific neural networks for X-ray to volume registration.
items.body: Advanced navigation techniques in image-guided interventions and surgical robotics require the rapid and precise alignment of three-dimensional (3D) preoperative volumes (such as computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging) to two-dimensional (2D) intraoperative images (such as X-ray fluoroscopy). However, existing 2D/3D registration methods fail to generalize across the broad spectrum of fluoroscopy-guided procedures: intensity-based optimizers require per-individual hyperparameter tuning, while deep-learning approaches demand extensive manually labelled datasets and remain constrained to the specific anatomy on which they were trained. Here, to address these limitations, we present xvr-a self-supervised framework that combines patient-specific neural networks with gradient-based optimization for automatic 2D/3D registration. xvr uses physics-based simulation to generate training data from a patient's own preoperative scan, eliminating the need for manual annotation. We present a foundation model pretrained on thousands of whole-body scans, achieving patient-specific adaptation to any anatomical region with only 5 min of fine-tuning. In to our knowledge the largest evaluation of 2D/3D registration on real fluoroscopy to date, xvr achieves high accuracy in seconds across diverse anatomical structures, volumetric imaging modalities and hospitals, improving on the accuracy of existing methods by an order of magnitude. xvr makes pan-anatomical 2D/3D rigid registration accessible to broad clinical and research communities through open-source software available online.
items.why: This Nature paper presents xvr, a self-supervised framework combining patient-specific neural networks with physics-based simulation to register two-dimensional (2D) intraoperative X-ray images to three-dimensional (3D) preoperative scans, pretrained as a foundation model on thousands of whole-body scans and fine-tuned in five minutes per anatomical region; in the largest reported evaluation of 2D/3D registration on real fluoroscopy, it improved accuracy by an order of magnitude over existing methods across hospitals and anatomies. This is a genuine technical first that removes the need for manual annotation and per-case tuning in image-guided surgery, with open-source release supporting broad generalizability, though its relevance to this reader is indirect since it is not reproductive-specific.
items.plain: Scientists built an AI system that can quickly and accurately line up a patient's live X-ray images during surgery with their earlier 3D CT or MRI scan, using simulated training data from the patient's own scan instead of requiring humans to label anything. Tested on real surgical X-rays from multiple hospitals, it was about ten times more accurate than previous methods and only needs a few minutes of extra training per body part, making it a strong step toward more precise, image-guided surgery.

glossary.definition: A way of training AI where the system creates its own training signal from data, rather than needing humans to label examples.
A large AI model trained on huge amounts of data that can be adapted to many different tasks, rather than being built for just one job.
A type of continuous X-ray imaging used to guide procedures in real time.
The process of aligning two different images or scans, such as a live X-ray and an earlier 3D scan, so they match up correctly.

items.title: Sex-specific biological aging clocks across organs and omics.
items.body: Sex differentially shapes aging, neurodevelopment and neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, most biological aging clocks (artificial intelligence-predicted age minus chronological age) were trained on sex-pooled samples and implicitly assume sex invariance.Here we developed 38 sex-specific biological aging clocks across 15 organ systems. We first demonstrate the importance of sex-stratified training for constructing sex-specific healthy normative references and then reveal marked divergence between female and male clocks. Key genetic parameters and Mendelian randomization results indicate that organ-specific aging liability and its relationships to cardiometabolic, endocrine and mental traits are configured differently in females and males. Proteomic analyses identify distinct, organ-resolved synaptic, immune, vascular and metabolic networks that differentially track female and male biological aging. In longitudinal survival analyses, sex-specific clocks predict whole-body systemic diseases and all-cause mortality in a sex-dependent and organ-dependent manner. Further analyses reveal sex-dependent associations between the brain aging clock and cognitive decline trajectory during a preclinical AD clinical trial. Sex-stratified clocks may offer distinct value by defining biological age against sex-appropriate normative references and revealing sex-dependent genetic, molecular and clinical signatures that pooled models may obscure. Meanwhile, sex-pooled and sex-interaction approaches remain valuable, as human aging and disease also share fundamental biological similarities between females and males. Together, these findings reveal sex-specific biological aging signatures in aging, AD and systemic health, highlighting the need for explicitly sex-stratified modeling approaches.
items.why: This Nature Medicine study built 38 sex-specific biological aging clocks, meaning artificial intelligence (AI) models predicting biological age from omics data, across 15 organ systems, using genetic, proteomic, and longitudinal survival analyses to show that organ aging relates differently to disease and mortality in females versus males, including sex-dependent links between brain aging and cognitive decline in a preclinical Alzheimer's disease (AD) trial. This is a large, methodologically rigorous demonstration that sex-pooled aging models can obscure clinically relevant biology, which matters for any AI-based risk model touching endocrine or hormone-sensitive systems, though it stops short of a prospective clinical intervention.
items.plain: Researchers built separate AI models to estimate the biological age of different organs for men and women, using genetic and protein data from large studies, and found that aging patterns and their links to disease and death differ by sex. This suggests that AI health-risk tools which don't account for sex differences could be missing important signals, though this study itself is observational and does not test a new treatment.

glossary.definition: An AI model that estimates how old a person's body or organ appears based on biological data, which can differ from their actual age in years.
Relating to the large-scale study of proteins in the body, often used to find patterns linked to disease.
Describes a study that follows the same people over time, rather than looking at them at just one moment.
A progressive brain disease that causes memory loss and cognitive decline, most common in older adults.

items.title: On-premise medical AI agents for reliable clinical decision-making.
items.body: Autonomous clinical artificial intelligence (AI) agents powered by large language models (LLMs), meaning systems that can complete a diagnostic workflow without continuous human input, are increasingly capable of supporting complex reasoning and decision-making. Clinical translation, however, remains limited by two unmet requirements: institutionally governed deployment and reliable decision-time uncertainty estimation. Here we developed and evaluated a fully on-premise clinical agent that couples local operational control with a multi-perspective reliability framework to support selective autonomy. Across two Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV)-derived benchmarks, the agent achieved 90.04% accuracy on a seven-disease task and 83.8% accuracy on a four-disease task, approaching a cloud baseline on the primary benchmark. To assess decision-time reliability, we quantified internal-likelihood, language-based and behavioral-stability measures for diagnosis and reasoning. Diagnostic behavioral consistency provided the strongest discrimination of correctness (area under the curve (AUC) = 0.860) and remained informative under stress testing (AUC = 0.875). At a consistency threshold of 0.90, 49.4% of cases were retained at 98.9% diagnostic accuracy. These findings support a practical framework for institutionally governed clinical agents in which decision-time reliability signals identify a lower-risk subset for autonomous handling and defer the remainder for review.
items.why: This Nat Med study developed a fully on-premise clinical agent powered by large language models (LLMs) that combines local institutional control with a multi-perspective reliability framework, achieving 90.04% and 83.8% accuracy on two Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV)-derived diagnostic benchmarks, with diagnostic behavioral consistency reaching an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.860-0.875 for identifying likely-correct cases. This offers a practical selective-autonomy framework for institutionally governed AI agents, but the evaluation relies on retrospective benchmark tasks rather than real-time deployment on live patients.
items.plain: Researchers built an AI clinical assistant that runs entirely within a hospital's own computers rather than the cloud, and tested how reliably it could diagnose conditions using a public intensive care database, getting the diagnosis right up to 90% of the time on one task. They also built a way to flag when the AI's answer is likely trustworthy versus when a human should double check, but this was tested on existing recorded cases rather than on real, live patients.

items.title: Real-time gestational-age estimation at 11-13 weeks using artificial intelligence on non-targeted ultrasound sweeps.
items.body: OBJECTIVE: To assess the accuracy of gestational-age estimation using an artificial intelligence (AI) system applied to non-targeted ultrasound sweeps at 11 + 0 to 13 + 6 weeks' gestation. METHODS: This was an observational study of singleton pregnancies undergoing routine first-trimester ultrasound in July 2025 to August 2025. Gestational age was estimated using crown-rump length (CRL), measured independently by two experienced sonographers blinded to the other's results, and by an AI system applied twice per examination. Comparisons were made using mean absolute error (MAE) and Bland-Altman analysis. A hierarchical measurement error model was used to account for uncertainty in CRL-based estimates and to estimate accuracy relative to a latent true gestational age, with Bayesian inference. RESULTS: Overall, 285 women with a singleton pregnancy were included. The AI model estimated gestational age in all cases, with a median acquisition time of 23 s for the first AI measurement. The MAE between AI- and CRL-based gestational age was 2.1 (95% CI, 1.9-2.3) days for single measurements and 2.0 days when averaging both AI estimates. Limits of agreement were wider for AI-based estimates than for CRL-based estimates, indicating lower precision. When accounting for measurement error in CRL, the estimated MAE for AI was lower (1.8 days for single and 1.6 days for duplicate measurements). CRL-based estimates showed lower variability than AI-based estimates. Within-operator variation was the main source of error in AI measurements. CONCLUSIONS: AI-based gestational-age estimation performs well in the first trimester but is less precise than gestational-age estimation using CRL measured by experienced sonographers. Measurement error models give a clearer picture of performance by accounting for variability in CRL and show that the accuracy of AI-based estimates is better than suggested by simple comparisons. © 2026 The Author(s). Ultrasound in Obstetrics & Gynecology published by John Wiley & Sons Ltd on behalf of International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology.
items.why: An observational study of 285 singleton pregnancies compared artificial intelligence (AI) based gestational-age estimation from non-targeted ultrasound sweeps against crown-rump length (CRL) measured by experienced sonographers, finding a mean absolute error (MAE) of about 2 days for AI versus higher precision for CRL, with a Bayesian hierarchical measurement-error model showing AI performance is better than naive comparisons suggest. This points toward simplified, less operator-dependent first-trimester dating that could extend access in lower-resource settings, though the AI system remains less precise than expert sonography and needs prospective validation against outcomes.
items.plain: Researchers tested an AI tool that estimates how many weeks pregnant someone is just from a quick, non-targeted ultrasound scan, comparing it to the standard method where a trained sonographer carefully measures the embryo. The AI was accurate to within about 2 days on average, a bit less precise than the expert measurement, but a special statistical method showed the AI was actually better than it first appeared, suggesting this could someday make early dating easier and faster.

A statistical approach that updates estimates of what is likely true by combining prior knowledge with new data, along with a measure of uncertainty.
A statistical model that accounts for the fact that even the reference method used for comparison has its own imprecision, giving a more accurate picture of true performance.

items.title: Large Language Models in Multidisciplinary Decision-Making for Hepatopancreatobiliary Oncology: Retrospective Comparative Feasibility Study.
items.body: BACKGROUND: Hepatopancreatobiliary (HPB) malignancies require complex treatment planning that often relies on multidisciplinary team (MDT) discussions. Large language models (LLMs) have recently been explored for clinical decision support, but their performance within real-world multidisciplinary decision environments remains unclear. In particular, the stability of LLM-generated recommendations-that is, whether a model produces the same answer when given the same clinical input-has rarely been examined. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the stability of treatment recommendations generated by contemporary LLMs when identical HPB cases are queried repeatedly, and their concordance with the treatment decisions reached at an institutional MDT conference. METHODS: This retrospective study included consecutive cases discussed at a single-center HPB MDT conference between September 1, 2024, and August 31, 2025. Standardized clinical case summaries derived from preconference documentation were provided to 4 LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Pro, and Claude Sonnet 4.5) through their consumer web interfaces. Each model recommended a treatment among predefined MDT treatment options, and identical queries were repeated 4 times in separate sessions. Stability was quantified as the discordance rate relative to the initial response and, without privileging any single query, as the mean pairwise agreement and Fleiss κ across the 4 iterations. Concordance with MDT decisions was assessed using both the initial and modal responses, together with Cohen κ and class-wise-scores. RESULTS: A total of 107 MDT cases were analyzed. Stability differed significantly across models (=.01). Gemini 3 Pro showed the lowest discordance rate (mean 12.8%, SD 2.3%) and the highest reference-free agreement (Fleiss κ=0.737), whereas GPT-4o showed the highest discordance rate (mean 30.2%, SD 6.5%) and the lowest agreement (Fleiss κ=0.430). Concordance with MDT decisions ranged from 48.6% to 72.9% using the initial response and from 66.3% to 74.5% using the modal response, and the highest-performing model differed between the 2 definitions. Class-wise-score was consistently lower for surgery (0.400-0.520) than for chemotherapy (0.621-0.836). Complete discordance occurred in 17 of 107 (15.9%) cases and in none of the 31 anatomically unresectable cases (Fisher exact test,=.003). Recurrent or on-treatment disease (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 5.40, 95% CI 1.65-17.68;=.005), pancreatic tumor location (adjusted OR 7.37, 95% CI 2.03-26.78;=.002), and low MDT agreement level (adjusted OR 10.33, 95% CI 1.54-69.38;=.016) were independently associated with complete discordance. CONCLUSIONS: LLM-generated treatment recommendations demonstrated moderate alignment with MDT decisions in HPB oncology. Importantly, response stability varied substantially across models, indicating that concordance alone is insufficient for evaluating LLMs as clinical decision support tools. These findings suggest that LLMs may serve as a reasoning-support layer in MDT-like decision environments, but their response stability must be systematically characterized before clinical integration.
items.why: This retrospective study fed 107 real hepatopancreatobiliary (HPB) cancer cases to four large language models (LLMs) repeatedly and measured both the stability of their treatment recommendations (using Fleiss kappa agreement across repeated queries) and their concordance with actual institutional multidisciplinary team (MDT) treatment decisions, finding concordance ranging from 48.6% to 74.5% and notable model-to-model variability in consistency. This goes beyond simple rubric grading by directly comparing LLM output against real clinical decision-making and quantifying reproducibility, a meaningful step for understanding LLM reliability in complex oncologic decision support.
items.plain: Researchers tested whether AI chatbots could match the treatment decisions that a real team of cancer specialists made for complex liver and pancreas cancer cases, and also checked whether the AI gave the same answer if asked the same question multiple times. The chatbots agreed with the human specialists' decisions only 49 to 75 percent of the time, and some models gave inconsistent answers when asked repeatedly, which is important because unreliable AI advice in complicated cancer cases could be risky.

items.title: A novel multiomics machine learning signature identifies rapid progression in clinically low risk prostate cancer.
items.body: Risk stratification in primary prostate cancer remains heavily reliant on clinicopathological criteria that frequently miss the heterogeneity underlying early aggressive disease. We present a novel machine learning non-linear prognostic framework encoding somatic copy-number alterations and biological information associated with gene products, along with an integrative multi-omics approach including epigenomics and transcriptomics into a patient-specific biological network. Applied to the TCGA-PRAD (n = 498), our weighted graph-based feature selection and LASSO-Cox model identified ZNF268 as a master regulator gene, in which the hypermethylation of its promoter region is linked to a distinct oncogenic transition exclusive to Low/Intermediate-risk disease. Post-hoc analysis of Low-ZNF268 tumors showed a distinct somatic landscape enriched for driver mutations and predicted sensitivity to MAPK, ATR, and PI3K/mTOR inhibitors, providing potential therapeutic vulnerabilities alongside the prognostic signal. Topological network analysis further revealed that ZNF268 loss impacts a co-expression rewiring gene network, quantified as a Rewiring Score: associated with Progression-Free Survival in the TCGA-PRAD (HR: 2.79, 95% CI: 1.36-5.71, p = 0.0049) and Biochemical Recurrence in two external cohorts. By capturing tumors at an active molecular transition state preceding systemic progression, this framework offers a prognostic tool to identify biologically aggressive prostate cancer disease within patients currently undertreated by standard risk criteria.
items.why: This NPJ Digital Medicine study used a weighted graph-based feature selection and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO)-Cox model on The Cancer Genome Atlas Prostate Adenocarcinoma (TCGA-PRAD) cohort (n=498) to identify ZNF268 hypermethylation as a marker of rapid progression in low/intermediate-risk prostate cancer, with the resulting Rewiring Score associated with progression-free survival (hazard ratio 2.79, 95% confidence interval 1.36-5.71) and validated for biochemical recurrence in two external cohorts. The multi-omics integration and external validation add credibility beyond a typical single-cohort model, but the work remains exploratory biomarker discovery rather than a clinically deployed tool.

items.title: Evaluating large language models for lay summaries of radiology reports using tailored prompting strategies and mixed-method assessment.
items.body: Radiology reports are often filled with medical jargon that limits patient understanding. Lay summaries can improve understanding but are time-consuming for healthcare providers to create. The objective of this study is to explore the use of tailored prompts for five Large Language Models (LLMs) in generating lay summaries from radiology reports. Using 100 reports from the publicly available "BioNLP 2023 report summarization" dataset, lay summaries were generated by each LLM, under select prompting styles [Few-Shot (GPT-4), Generated Knowledge (GPT-4o mini, Gemini 1.5 - Pro, Gemini 1.5 - Flash), and Zero-Shot (Llama 3.1)] informed by a pilot work. The summaries were evaluated using a mixed-method framework: subjective assessment (Likert statements) by blinded experts (n = 2 radiology fellows) and Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) [(Gemini 2.5 - Pro (LRM 1); GPT-oss-120b (LRM 2)], and readability metrics (Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level and Flesch Reading Ease). Using percentage agreement of Likert statements, the LLM-prompt combinations' performances were ranked, and Friedman and post-hoc Nemenyi tests were conducted. Gemini 1.5 - Flash and - Pro (generated knowledge) were rated highest by human experts and LRMs for generating actionable lay summaries that require minimal supervision [P < 4.97 × 10-2 (Rater 1); P < 9.03 × 10-21 (Rater 2), P < 6.90 × 10-15 (LRM 1), P < 2.760 × 10-5 (LRM 2). GPT-4 (few-shot) achieved the highest human-rated accuracy (98%), while Gemini 1.5 - Flash (LRM 1-rated: 95%) and Gemini 1.5 - Pro (LRM 2-rated: 91%) ranked first in LRM-rated accuracy. Gemini 1.5 - Pro produced the most accessible summaries (Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level: 7.55 ± 1.38, Flesch Reading Ease: 67.84 ± 7.78). Strong agreement was observed between experts and LRMs [0.96% (LRM 1) and 3.4% (LRM 2) complete disagreement]. Overall, this study highlights Gemini-models with generated knowledge prompts and the potential of LRM evaluators in assessing LLM-generated lay summaries.
items.why: This study tested five large language models (LLMs) generating lay summaries of 100 real radiology reports from a public dataset, using tailored prompting strategies and evaluating quality through both blinded radiology fellow ratings and large reasoning model (LRM) evaluators alongside readability metrics like Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level. The inclusion of human expert ratings alongside automated evaluators and a focus on real report content makes this a somewhat more rigorous evaluation than typical rubric-only chatbot studies, though it lacks a comparison against clinician-written summaries or actual patient comprehension testing.
items.plain: Researchers had several AI models turn complicated radiology reports into plain-language summaries, then had radiology doctors and other AI systems judge how good those summaries were, and measured how easy they were to read. One version of the AI produced the clearest and most accurate summaries, but the study did not test whether real patients actually understood better as a result.

scored.title: An expert-level generalist AI for abdominal CT diagnosis.
scored.why: This Science paper reports RADAR, a generalist vision-language model trained on more than 400,000 contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography (CT) exams and 15 million anatomy-wise image-text pairs without manual annotation, which achieved high diagnostic performance across 18 anatomical structures and 146 findings in multicenter internal and external evaluations, and increased the diagnostic sensitivity of 26 radiologists by about 10% in a reader study. This is a substantial, well-validated advance in generalist radiology AI with a real clinician-comparison reader study, making it one of the strongest clinical AI results of the week even though it sits outside reproductive medicine.

scored.why: This prospective observational study tracked all 2035 real patient conversations (6146 messages) with a deployed retrieval-augmented generative artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot for Parkinson's disease information in Germany over 129 days, using a structured surveillance framework (CARE-LLM) combining automated triage and expert review; while 88.6% of conversations were rated good, independent re-review found clinically critical errors in 4% of

scored.title: The Virtual Biotech: A multi-agent AI framework for therapeutic discovery and development.
scored.why: This Science paper introduces the Virtual Biotech, a multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) system in which over 37,000 agents modeled on drug-development roles annotated outcomes from 55,984 trials, finding that drugs targeting cell-type-specific genes were 48% more likely to reach market with 32% fewer adverse events, and it further demonstrated utility in proposing a lung cancer therapeutic strategy and diagnosing a failed ulcerative colitis trial. The scale and transparency of this multi-agent reasoning approach is a notable methodological first for drug development, though the trial-outcome associations are retrospective and correlational rather than prospectively validated.

scored.title: Rapid patient-specific neural networks for X-ray to volume registration.
scored.why: This Nature paper presents xvr, a self-supervised framework combining patient-specific neural networks with physics-based simulation to register two-dimensional (2D) intraoperative X-ray images to three-dimensional (3D) preoperative scans, pretrained as a foundation model on thousands of whole-body scans and fine-tuned in five minutes per anatomical region; in the largest reported evaluation of 2D/3D registration on real fluoroscopy, it improved accuracy by an order of magnitude over existing methods across hospitals and anatomies. This is a genuine technical first that removes the need for manual annotation and per-case tuning in image-guided surgery, with open-source release supporting broad generalizability, though its relevance to this reader is indirect since it is not reproductive-specific.

scored.title: Sex-specific biological aging clocks across organs and omics.
scored.why: This Nature Medicine study built 38 sex-specific biological aging clocks, meaning artificial intelligence (AI) models predicting biological age from omics data, across 15 organ systems, using genetic, proteomic, and longitudinal survival analyses to show that organ aging relates differently to disease and mortality in females versus males, including sex-dependent links between brain aging and cognitive decline in a preclinical Alzheimer's disease (AD) trial. This is a large, methodologically rigorous demonstration that sex-pooled aging models can obscure clinically relevant biology, which matters for any AI-based risk model touching endocrine or hormone-sensitive systems, though it stops short of a prospective clinical intervention.

scored.title: On-premise medical AI agents for reliable clinical decision-making.
scored.why: This Nat Med study developed a fully on-premise clinical agent powered by large language models (LLMs) that combines local institutional control with a multi-perspective reliability framework, achieving 90.04% and 83.8% accuracy on two Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV)-derived diagnostic benchmarks, with diagnostic behavioral consistency reaching an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.860-0.875 for identifying likely-correct cases. This offers a practical selective-autonomy framework for institutionally governed AI agents, but the evaluation relies on retrospective benchmark tasks rather than real-time deployment on live patients.

scored.title: Real-time gestational-age estimation at 11-13 weeks using artificial intelligence on non-targeted ultrasound sweeps.
scored.why: An observational study of 285 singleton pregnancies compared artificial intelligence (AI) based gestational-age estimation from non-targeted ultrasound sweeps against crown-rump length (CRL) measured by experienced sonographers, finding a mean absolute error (MAE) of about 2 days for AI versus higher precision for CRL, with a Bayesian hierarchical measurement-error model showing AI performance is better than naive comparisons suggest. This points toward simplified, less operator-dependent first-trimester dating that could extend access in lower-resource settings, though the AI system remains less precise than expert sonography and needs prospective validation against outcomes.

scored.title: Large Language Models in Multidisciplinary Decision-Making for Hepatopancreatobiliary Oncology: Retrospective Comparative Feasibility Study.
scored.why: This retrospective study fed 107 real hepatopancreatobiliary (HPB) cancer cases to four large language models (LLMs) repeatedly and measured both the stability of their treatment recommendations (using Fleiss kappa agreement across repeated queries) and their concordance with actual institutional multidisciplinary team (MDT) treatment decisions, finding concordance ranging from 48.6% to 74.5% and notable model-to-model variability in consistency. This goes beyond simple rubric grading by directly comparing LLM output against real clinical decision-making and quantifying reproducibility, a meaningful step for understanding LLM reliability in complex oncologic decision support.

scored.title: Intuitive single-port robot earns CE mark for new indication
scored.why: Intuitive's single-port da Vinci SP surgical robot received a CE mark for transvaginal gynecologic procedures, expanding its approved indications in Europe. This is a concrete regulatory clearance for a named device with a direct gynecologic application, meeting the bar for solid industry news even without efficacy data attached.

scored.title: A novel multiomics machine learning signature identifies rapid progression in clinically low risk prostate cancer.
scored.why: This NPJ Digital Medicine study used a weighted graph-based feature selection and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO)-Cox model on The Cancer Genome Atlas Prostate Adenocarcinoma (TCGA-PRAD) cohort (n=498) to identify ZNF268 hypermethylation as a marker of rapid progression in low/intermediate-risk prostate cancer, with the resulting Rewiring Score associated with progression-free survival (hazard ratio 2.79, 95% confidence interval 1.36-5.71) and validated for biochemical recurrence in two external cohorts. The multi-omics integration and external validation add credibility beyond a typical single-cohort model, but the work remains exploratory biomarker discovery rather than a clinically deployed tool.

scored.title: Evaluating large language models for lay summaries of radiology reports using tailored prompting strategies and mixed-method assessment.
scored.why: This study tested five large language models (LLMs) generating lay summaries of 100 real radiology reports from a public dataset, using tailored prompting strategies and evaluating quality through both blinded radiology fellow ratings and large reasoning model (LRM) evaluators alongside readability metrics like Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level. The inclusion of human expert ratings alongside automated evaluators and a focus on real report content makes this a somewhat more rigorous evaluation than typical rubric-only chatbot studies, though it lacks a comparison against clinician-written summaries or actual patient comprehension testing.

scored.title: How appropriate are ChatGPT-5's answers to acne questions?: A category-based evaluation by dermatologists.
scored.why: Three dermatologists blindly rated 75 ChatGPT-5 responses to 25 common acne questions as appropriate or inappropriate, finding 65.3% appropriate overall but only 33.3% appropriate for diagnosis questions, with low inter-rater agreement. This is a rubric-style evaluation without a clinician comparator, but the category-specific failure breakdown (worse performance on diagnosis and treatment than skincare) offers modestly useful signal about where chatbot advice is riskiest.

scored.title: Large language models for tympanostomy patient education: readability and guideline adherence.
scored.why: This study compared ChatGPT 4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Google Search AI on a 12-point rubric adapted from American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery (AAO-HNS) Clinical Practice Guidelines for tympanostomy tube patient education, finding Gemini and Google Search AI outperformed ChatGPT on guideline adherence but all outputs exceeded recommended reading level. It has no clinician-versus-model comparison on real patient interactions and is a narrow single-topic benchmark, making it routine for this beat rather than field-changing.

scored.title: Differentiating high- and low-grade serous ovarian carcinoma using radiomics: a pilot study.
scored.why: This single-center retrospective pilot study of 153 patients extracted ultrasound radiomics features and built logistic regression models to distinguish high-grade from low-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, reporting area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUC) with only internal bootstrap validation. It is a small, single-institution proof-of-concept without external validation, so it is informative but not yet clinically actionable.

scored.title: Assessing the accuracy and readability of large language models in answering Turkish-language patient-generated queries on radiological contrast agents.
scored.why: This study had three large language models (LLMs) answer 30 popular Turkish patient questions about radiological contrast agents, scoring clinical accuracy against American College of Radiology (ACR) guidelines and quality using the Ensuring Quality Information for Patients (EQIP-36) scale, finding Claude 4.6 Sonnet most accurate while all models lacked source citations. This is a rubric-based accuracy evaluation without a clinician comparator or patient outcome measure, so it is informative but routine for this beat.

scored.title: Assessing the accuracy and usability of artificial intelligence-based language models in responding to common periodontal patient questions.
scored.why: This comparative study had two board-certified periodontists rate responses from ten large language models (LLMs) to 15 periodontal patient questions in English and Persian on a 5-point Likert scale across accuracy, clarity, and usability, finding ChatGPT-4.5 with deep search performed best and usability for low-literacy patients scored lowest. This is a routine rubric-based comparison without a clinician-response comparator or real patient interaction, limiting its novelty for this beat.

scored.title: Comparative evaluation of ChatGPT and gemini responses to patient-oriented questions on breast cancer.
scored.why: Four general surgeons blindly rated ChatGPT and Gemini responses to 40 patient-oriented breast cancer questions on scientific accuracy, clarity, and unnecessary detail, finding ChatGPT scored significantly higher on all measures. This is a head-to-head chatbot comparison using expert rubric scoring without a human clinician response comparator or measure of patient understanding, making it routine for this beat.

scored.title: Attitudes Toward Large Language Models in Health Care and Preferences for Their Adoption and Oversight Among Health Care Professionals: Cross-Sectional Survey.
scored.why: This cross-sectional survey of 335 health care professionals, recruited via a health care news mailing list, found 62.7% reported current or contemplated large language model (LLM) use, with most valuing patient communication and literature review but expressing high concern about bias and low confidence in oversight. It is self-reported attitudinal data with a low response rate and non-representative convenience sample, so it offers context on clinician sentiment rather than evidence about actual model performance or patient outcomes.

scored.title: Do bots provide correct and adequate guidance regarding acidity: A blinded comparison rated by patients and physicians.
scored.why: This blinded comparison had three gastroenterologists and 20 patients rate responses from ChatGPT-5, Gemini-2.5, and Claude-4 to 39 patient questions about heartburn and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), finding Gemini and Claude outperformed ChatGPT on accuracy and actionability while ChatGPT was more readable. It includes both clinician and patient raters, which is a step up from pure rubric scoring, but remains a single-condition comparative benchmark without real patient interactions or workflow impact.

scored.title: Safety guardrails in patient-facing large language model systems for chronic disease self-management: a realist review.
scored.why: This realist review synthesized 21 studies and 38 context-mechanism-outcome configurations (CMOCs) on safety guardrails in patient-facing large language model (LLM) systems for chronic disease self-management, concluding that most evidence involves simulated or single-turn interactions rather than sustained real-world deployment. As a review with no new primary data and an explicit call for real-world longitudinal testing, it is useful framing but not a new empirical finding for this beat.

scored.title: Patient-facing generative artificial intelligence: interpretive influence and system-level evaluation.
scored.why: This Lancet Digital Health paper is announced by title only, addressing patient-facing generative artificial intelligence (AI) and its interpretive influence, with no abstract or study details provided. Without a description of methodology, comparator, or effect size, it cannot be judged as evidence and is scored conservatively for lack of substance.

scored.title: Sustainable artificial intelligence in global health: balancing promise, equity, and environmental realities in low- and middle-income countries.
scored.why: This is a perspective piece from an informatics working group proposing a framework (Green AI assessments, workflow-integrated evaluation, federated governance) for sustainable artificial intelligence (AI) deployment in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), without new data or an evaluated system. It offers conceptual guidance rather than evidence of a clinical or research advance, so it has limited value for a reader tracking substantive results.

scored.title: Machine learning-based identification of core regulatory targets in 1-nitropyrene-induced placental trophoblast dysfunction and FGR.
scored.why: This mouse and cell-culture study used machine learning simply as a gene-selection filter to identify candidate genes (CPS1, ERRFI1, GSTA4, HK2) linking the pollutant 1-nitropyrene to fetal growth restriction (FGR) via trophoblast dysfunction, with mechanistic validation but no clinical AI application. It belongs to reproductive toxicology and molecular biology rather than clinical AI in reproductive medicine, so it is off-topic for this reader's core interests despite the reproductive subject matter.

scored.title: Biomarker-driven diagnostics and personalized treatment in polycystic ovary syndrome.
scored.why: This review of biomarker-driven diagnostics for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) discusses hormonal, metabolic, and molecular markers and mentions artificial intelligence-assisted diagnostic models only briefly as showing high predictive performance, without presenting original data. As a review with minimal AI substance, it offers limited new information for this reader.

scored.title: Readability of National Institutes of Health Patient Education Materials Focused on Mental Health.
scored.why: This cross-sectional study compared readability metrics (Flesch-Kincaid, Gunning Fog, and others) of National Institutes of Health (NIH) mental health patient education materials as scored by a readability tool versus two large language model (LLM) chatbots, finding materials generally exceed recommended reading levels. There is no patient interaction, clinician comparator, or effect on understanding measured, making this a routine readability audit rather than a substantive contribution to patient-facing AI evaluation.

scored.title: Implementing a Domain-Adapted GPT Model to Support Genetic Counseling in a Genodermatology Clinic.
scored.why: The title describes implementation of a domain-adapted generative pre-trained transformer (GPT) model to support genetic counseling in a genodermatology clinic, but no abstract text is available to assess study design, evaluation methods, or findings. Without substantive details, this cannot be scored as a meaningful contribution this week.

scored.title: AI-Enabled Prescribing in Opioid Use Disorder Care: Decision Support, Risk Scores, Large Language Model Copilots, and Digital Therapeutics (2024-2025).
scored.why: This is a narrative, practice-oriented review mapping the 2024-2025 landscape of AI-enabled tools in opioid use disorder (OUD) prescribing, covering decision support, prescription drug monitoring program (PDMP) analytics, large language model (LLM) copilots, and digital therapeutics, without presenting original data or evaluation. As a review synthesizing existing tools and regulatory frameworks rather than reporting a new study, it is low priority despite covering a relevant clinical AI topic.

scored.title: Large Language Models for Clinical Note Simplification: A Systematic Review and Experimental Evaluation of Medical Text Readability.
scored.why: This study combined a systematic literature review with an experimental test of ten large language models (LLMs) simplifying five synthetic German clinical notes, evaluated using standard readability indices like Flesch Reading Ease and a novel measure of medical terminology density. The evaluation used only synthetic notes rather than real patient records or clinician comparison, and readability scores alone do not establish whether patients actually understand the simplified text better.

scored.title: How a Cancer Diagnosis Shaped This VC’s Precision Health Thesis
scored.why: This is a profile piece on a venture capitalist who co-founded a precision health and longevity fund after her own cancer diagnosis, with the fund having backed 83 early-stage startups over three years. It contains no specific deal, product, or regulatory news and no clear women's health angle beyond the founder's personal story, making it thought-leadership rather than concrete industry movement.

scored.title: Multi-organelle signatures map cell-state diversity and metabolic adaptation in tissues.
scored.why: This Science paper describes sOrganellomics, an imaging and machine learning workflow that classifies cell states from organelle structure in liver and pancreas tissue, revealing subzonal hepatocyte diversity and fasting-induced organelle remodeling. It is a basic cell biology tool with no patient-facing, diagnostic, or clinical decision-making component, so it falls outside the scope of clinical AI, reproductive AI, or patient-facing language model beats.

scored.title: The evolving role of immunotherapy in ovarian cancer.
scored.why: This is a narrative review of immunotherapy strategies in ovarian cancer that mentions artificial intelligence and machine learning only briefly as an emerging tool for integrating multimodal data for response prediction. It contains no new study, data, or AI methodology, so it offers little for a reader tracking substantive clinical AI advances.

scored.title: Epigenetic mechanisms and clinical translation in ovarian cancer: from molecular pathways to precision therapy.
scored.why: This narrative review covers epigenetic mechanisms of ovarian cancer drug resistance and mentions artificial intelligence-based liquid biopsy platforms only in passing as a future direction. No original AI methodology or data is presented, making it low priority for this beat.

scored.title: Air pollution and autism-like traits: Sensitive periods and joint effects of exposure to sources and constituents of fine particulate matter.
scored.why: This cohort study used machine learning land-use regression models only to estimate residential air pollution exposure, then examined associations between particulate matter constituents and autism-like traits in 798 children using distributed lag and single-index models. The AI component is a minor exposure-modeling tool rather than a clinical AI application, and the topic (environmental epidemiology of autism) falls outside the reproductive, clinical AI, or patient-communication beats.

scored.title: Prenatal exposure to particulate matter and risk of autism spectrum disorder in children: a population-based cohort study in South Korea.
scored.why: This nationwide South Korean cohort of nearly 700,000 mother-child pairs used machine learning-based air pollution exposure models and Cox proportional hazards regression to test associations between prenatal particulate matter and autism spectrum disorder (ASD), finding no significant associations. The AI use is limited to exposure estimation rather than any clinical or reproductive AI application, placing it outside this reader's core beats despite its large scale.

scored.title: Evaluating AI Chatbots in Prosthodontics Education: A Quantitative MCQ-Based Assessment.
scored.why: This study evaluated four chatbots' accuracy on 150 multiple-choice prosthodontics exam questions using text-similarity metrics like bilingual evaluation understudy (BLEU) score and readability indices, which tests exam performance rather than patient communication. It has no patient interaction or clinical deployment component, so it falls outside the scope of this beat.

scored.title: Characterizing LLM scientific concept generation: A multi-dimensional measurement study.
scored.why: This paper characterizes text outputs from seven large language models (LLMs) across five scientific domains using measures like coherence, readability, and semantic embedding position, explicitly avoiding claims about clinical relevance or patient interaction. It has no connection to patient communication, clinical evaluation, or health outcomes and is off-topic for this beat.
